title: edge-proxy-burst-sim-scratch
content:
Goal:
Quick scratchpad to capture a weird tail-latency pattern observed when routing through the new edge-proxy (v0.8.2) during bursty ingress. Purpose is to capture test conditions, raw numbers, a tiny ascii chart, quick hypotheses, and next steps.

Context and why I care:
- Prod-like workload: short text generation (avg 24 tokens), strict p99 SLO (100ms).
- We roll traffic through the edge-proxy for connection pooling, TLS offload, header enrichment. It introduced a small additional hop.
- During a recent capacity test, p99 jumped from ~85ms to ~230ms for a narrow qps range (320-420 qps) only when proxy had request-level logging enabled. Direct-serving (no-proxy) did not show this spike.

Test harness (approx):
- Client: local load generator (k6 script) from bench-node-3, 50ms synthetic think time between users, Poisson arrivals.
- Targets: 
  * baseline: model-serving (direct) behind nginx LB (no edge proxy)
  * proxy: same target but fronted by edge-proxy (v0.8.2) with default keepalive
- Workload: single-route text-gen, input size ~24 tokens, model = redwood-small-1 (quantized), response size ~48 tokens.
- Concurrency limits: server max inflight 256, proxy connection pool size 200, proxy logger enabled vs disabled toggles.
- Sweep: QPS 50, 100, 200, 320, 360, 400, 420, 480, 600, 800, 1000
- Each point: 2m warmup + 6m measure, 95%CI observed but not exhaustive.

Key raw numbers (p50 / p95 / p99) — median of measurement window per QPS point:
- Baseline (no-proxy):
  50qps: 28 / 42 / 63 ms
  200qps: 33 / 58 / 92 ms
  320qps: 36 / 68 / 110 ms
  400qps: 40 / 75 / 123 ms
  800qps: 62 / 115 / 190 ms

- Proxy (logging OFF):
  50qps: 32 / 48 / 73 ms
  200qps: 38 / 64 / 105 ms
  320qps: 42 / 70 / 118 ms
  400qps: 48 / 85 / 140 ms
  800qps: 78 / 140 / 250 ms

- Proxy (logging ON):
  50qps: 36 / 58 / 96 ms
  200qps: 44 / 82 / 160 ms
  320qps: 58 / 150 / 320 ms  <-- big jump in this band
  360qps: 63 / 180 / 450 ms
  400qps: 68 / 220 / 520 ms
  420qps: 70 / 240 / 610 ms

Quick ASCII sketch (p99 vs QPS) — approximate:
QPS | p99(ms) (baseline / proxy-no-log / proxy-log)
-------------------------------------------------
 50 | 63 / 73 / 96
200 | 92 / 105 / 160
320 |110 /118 /320  <-- divergence
400 |123 /140 /520  <-- catastrophic tail
800 |190 /250 /610

Observations / immediate hypotheses:
1) Logging path + synchronous disk/network flush: enabling request-level logging in the proxy correlates with a non-linear tail spike concentrated in a narrow QPS band. Suspect log buffer pressure or periodic flush triggered by queue length.
2) Pooling interactions: proxy uses a small connection pool (200). At ~320-420 qps we may be hitting connection churn + backpressure causing head-of-line blocking.
3) TCP/H2 multiplexing + max-concurrency mismatch: if proxy multiplexes many small requests over a few backend connections, one slow backend request (e.g. GC pause) could block others.
4) CPU context switch / writer lock: proxy's logger shares a lock used by the I/O loop -> periodic stalls.
5) Not likely TLS CPU — disabled in both runs for parity.

What I checked quickly (not exhaustive):
- Confirmed proxy CPU utilization spiked modestly during the bad windows (35% -> 75% on 8-core), but not saturated.
- Backend model-serving CPU/GPU usage looked flat; no corresponding GC events in the backend JVM (we're not using JVM for serving but check agent).
- Swap, disk io on proxy host negligible (no swap).
- Packet counts show occasional retransmits in windows (small), no large packet loss.

Immediate remediation experiments to try next (ordered):
- Re-run with proxy logging ON but using async buffered logger (non-blocking). If tail goes away -> logging path culprit.
- Increase proxy connection pool to 800 and re-sweep. If tail moves right -> pooling backpressure.
- Reduce keepalive timeout to force faster churn and observe directionality.
- Add synthetic 5ms delay on a small fraction of backend requests to see amplification via multiplexing.
- Capture flame / eBPF traces of proxy during spike to find syscall blocking.

Quick TODOs (short):
- [ ] Re-run async-logger test (Maya to help with config) — target 2026-03-07
- [ ] Run connection-pool=800 sweep (Jordan) — target 2026-03-09
- [ ] Attach eBPF trace during next spike and share slice in GH gist
- [ ] If logging path confirmed, propose safe default: async logger + cap log rate + circuit-break logging backfill.

Notes for postmortem-ish doc if root cause confirmed:
- Impact window narrow but severe: some customers hitting p99 > 500ms for a few minutes during bursts.
- Root cause likely application-level blocking in proxy rather than backend serving. Fix in 0.8.3 release candidate.

Raw artifacts:
- k6 scripts: gist link (attached below)
- raw csv exports: /bench/outputs/edge-proxy-burst/2026-02-28/ (will copy to GH once triaged)

Gists / quick links: https://gist.github.com/jordan-k/edge-proxy-320-sweep (placeholder)

End notes: this is a working scratchpad — not complete. Keeping log of approximate numbers so we don't forget the narrow-band spike behavior.
